title: How a specialty shop runs on its till: an introduction to retail POS and store management
audience: A curious adult coming from a different field, with no assumed knowledge of retail or software.
scope: Covers the software that independent specialty shops, small chains and franchise formulas in the Netherlands and Belgium use to sell at the counter, manage stock, buy from suppliers, sell online and keep their books. Examples come from Vendit, one Dutch vendor that belongs to the Katapull software group. Restaurants, supermarkets and large department-store systems are left out.
learningGoals: Explain what a modern till system does beyond taking money.
Describe why stock accuracy matters for both the shop floor and the webshop.
Distinguish selling, stock, purchasing and reporting as separate but linked activities.
Explain why specialty branches such as bike shops need features general shops do not.
Name the main trade-offs a shop owner faces when choosing and switching systems.

introduction.whatItIs:
A retail point-of-sale (POS) and store management system is the software behind the till in a shop. It records each sale, but it also keeps the list of everything the shop sells, how many of each item are on the shelves, what they cost to buy, which customers are regulars, and what the day's numbers look like.

In a specialty shop - a bike shop, jeweller, outdoor store or hobby shop - the same system often also runs the repair workshop, the webshop and the orders sent to suppliers.
introduction.whyItMatters: Small shops compete with large online sellers on advice and service, not on scale. If the shop says "sold out" while the item sits in the back room, or the webshop sells something that is no longer there, it loses exactly the trust it depends on. The till system is where the shop's information either stays correct or quietly goes wrong.
introduction.familiarComparison: Think of it as the shop's memory and nervous system: every scan at the till is a signal that updates what the shop knows about its stock, money and customers.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: Unlike a memory, the system only knows what people and connected systems tell it. If deliveries are not scanned in, or a supplier sends outdated data, it will confidently report wrong facts.

participants.name: Shop owner
participants.role: Buys the system, decides on prices and assortment, carries the financial risk.
participants.caresAbout: Margin, stock tied up in money, time spent on admin, and not being let down on a busy Saturday.

participants.name: Sales associate
participants.role: Advises customers and works the till.
participants.caresAbout: A quick, error-free checkout and being able to tell a customer whether an item can be had.

participants.name: Workshop technician
participants.role: Repairs bikes, jewellery or devices that customers bring in.
participants.caresAbout: A clear plan, parts in stock, and customers who know when to come back.

participants.name: Head office of a chain or franchise formula
participants.role: Sets prices, campaigns and joint purchasing for many shops.
participants.caresAbout: That every shop executes the formula consistently.

participants.name: Supplier or wholesaler
participants.caresAbout: Receiving correct orders electronically and having its products described correctly in shops.

participants.name: Shopper
participants.role: Buys in store, on the webshop or on a marketplace.
participants.caresAbout: Availability, advice and easy service - they rarely know which software is behind it.

participants.name: Software vendor
participants.role: Builds, installs and supports the system, often including hardware.
participants.caresAbout: Shops that stay for years and grow into more modules.

concepts.meaning: The place and software where a sale is registered and paid.
concepts.example: Scanning a bike lock, applying a 10% loyalty discount and taking a card payment.
concepts.whyItMatters: It is the most frequent and time-critical moment in the shop; everything else depends on it being recorded correctly.

media.alt: Point of sale (POS): Scanning a bike lock, applying a 10% loyalty discount and taking a card payment.
media.caption: It is the most frequent and time-critical moment in the shop; everything else depends on it being recorded correctly.

concepts.meaning: The shop's list of every item it can sell, with barcode, price, supplier and description.
concepts.example: A helmet in three sizes is one article with three variants, each with its own barcode.
concepts.whyItMatters: The till, the webshop and the marketplaces all read from it; one mistake appears everywhere.

media.title: Article master
media.alt: Article master: A helmet in three sizes is one article with three variants, each with its own barcode.
media.caption: The till, the webshop and the marketplaces all read from it; one mistake appears everywhere.

concepts.meaning: The running record of how many of each item are where, changed by every sale, delivery, return and correction.
concepts.example: Selling one helmet in the Haarlem store lowers Haarlem stock by one and the webshop shows one fewer.
concepts.whyItMatters: Real-time stock is what lets a shop avoid saying "no" while the item is somewhere in the business.

media.title: Stock ledger
media.alt: Stock ledger: Selling one helmet in the Haarlem store lowers Haarlem stock by one and the webshop shows one fewer.
media.caption: Real-time stock is what lets a shop avoid saying "no" while the item is somewhere in the business.

concepts.meaning: The difference between what an item sells for and what it cost to buy, after discounts.
concepts.example: A EUR 100 jacket bought for EUR 55 gives EUR 45 margin, unless it is sold with a 20% discount.
concepts.whyItMatters: Turnover can grow while margin shrinks; owners steer on margin.

media.title: Margin
media.alt: Margin: A EUR 100 jacket bought for EUR 55 gives EUR 45 margin, unless it is sold with a 20% discount.
media.caption: Turnover can grow while margin shrinks; owners steer on margin.

concepts.meaning: A rule per item saying at what stock level to reorder and up to what level.
concepts.example: Inner tubes: reorder when fewer than 10, top up to 40.
concepts.whyItMatters: It turns daily sales into a purchase proposal instead of relying on memory.

media.title: Min/max replenishment
media.alt: Min/max replenishment: Inner tubes: reorder when fewer than 10, top up to 40.
media.caption: It turns daily sales into a purchase proposal instead of relying on memory.

concepts.meaning: Selling through several channels (shop, own webshop, marketplaces) from one stock and one customer view.
concepts.example: A tent listed in the shop, on the webshop and on bol, with one shared stock count.
concepts.whyItMatters: Without shared stock, channels oversell each other and customers receive cancellations.

media.title: Omnichannel
media.alt: Omnichannel: A tent listed in the shop, on the webshop and on bol, with one shared stock count.
media.caption: Without shared stock, channels oversell each other and customers receive cancellations.

concepts.meaning: Electronic exchange of product data, orders, delivery notes and invoices between shop and supplier. EDI (electronic data interchange) is a standardised form of this.
concepts.example: A bike shop orders from a wholesaler inside its till system and receives frame numbers with the delivery.
concepts.whyItMatters: It removes retyping, which is where many price and stock errors start.

media.alt: Supplier connection / EDI: A bike shop orders from a wholesaler inside its till system and receives frame numbers with the delivery.
media.caption: It removes retyping, which is where many price and stock errors start.

concepts.meaning: A chain of independently owned shops operating under one brand and shared rules.
concepts.example: Franchise stores of a household brand receiving prices and campaigns from a service organisation.
concepts.whyItMatters: Head office needs to publish centrally while each owner runs their own shop.

historyNote: A selective, Netherlands-focused view of how shop automation changed; dates are broad periods.

history.change: Electronic cash registers with barcode scanning replaced mechanical tills; small software firms began building PC-based till programs. Vendit traces its start to 1986.
history.whyItMatters: Sales started to become data that could update stock automatically.

history.change: PC-based systems added stock management, purchasing and links to accounting; branch associations and wholesalers started exchanging electronic product files.
history.whyItMatters: Specialty branches developed their own data standards and specialist vendors.

history.change: Webshops and marketplaces became normal sales channels for small shops; cloud hosting and monthly subscriptions replaced one-off licences.
history.whyItMatters: Stock had to be shared across channels in near real time.

history.change: Software groups formed by combining specialised vendors. In March 2025 Vendit joined Logic4, DeliveryMatch, EffectConnect and Highbiza in the Katapull group, which later added Transus, Returnista and Picqer.
history.whyItMatters: Shops can connect till, marketplaces, shipping and returns from one group of vendors, but face questions about which product fits as they grow.

walkthrough.title: A spring Saturday at a fictional bike shop
walkthrough.setup: Fictional example: Anna owns a two-branch bike shop. Her associate Tom works the till, Sven runs the workshop. The shop sells in store, on its own webshop and on one marketplace. Numbers are illustrative.

steps.title: Morning numbers
steps.whatHappens: Anna opens the dashboard on her phone: yesterday's turnover, margin and average receipt compared with last year.
steps.whyItMatters: She sees that discounts ate into margin and tells Tom to stop giving ad-hoc price reductions.

steps.title: A customer wants a specific e-bike
steps.whatHappens: Tom checks stock: none in this branch, one at the other branch. He reserves it and arranges a transfer.
steps.whyItMatters: Real-time stock across branches turns a "no" into a sale.
steps.watchOut: If the other branch sold it online ten minutes earlier and the sync is slow, the promise breaks.

steps.title: A repair comes in
steps.whatHappens: A customer brings a bike with brake problems. Tom registers a repair order on the customer's name with the frame number. Sven sees it on his planning board.
steps.whyItMatters: The repair cannot be lost, and parts used are taken from stock.

steps.title: Online orders and returns
steps.whatHappens: Two marketplace orders arrive in the system. Labels are printed from the till system; a returned helmet from last week is booked back into stock.
steps.whyItMatters: Online sales share the same stock, so nothing is sold twice.

steps.title: Exception: supplier price change
steps.whatHappens: A wholesaler raised purchase prices overnight. The supplier connection updates the article data, and the system flags items whose margin is now below target.
steps.whyItMatters: Without the connection, Anna would discover the margin loss weeks later.

steps.title: Closing the day
steps.whatHappens: Tom counts the drawer; it matches card and cash totals. The day's figures are prepared for the accountant. Overnight, the system proposes reorders based on min/max levels.
steps.whyItMatters: The books and stock are right before the next day starts.

walkthrough.outcome: The shop sold more without extra admin: the e-bike sale was saved, the repair was planned, online orders were shipped and margins were protected. Success for Anna is a calm Saturday evening; for the shopper it is getting what was promised.

valueAndIncentives.title: Who pays and how
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Shops pay a monthly subscription that depends on package, number of workstations and modules; vendors such as Vendit bundle hardware, installation, data migration and support into that fee.
valueAndIncentives.example: Vendit lists its entry POS package from about EUR 119-129 per month and a webshop module from EUR 299 per month (October 2026).

valueAndIncentives.title: Where the shop gains
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Fewer lost sales from stock errors, less time on admin, better buying decisions and extra online reach.
valueAndIncentives.example: An owner who stops retyping supplier price lists frees hours each week.

valueAndIncentives.title: Vendor incentives
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Vendors earn most from shops that stay for many years and add modules. Switching is costly for shops, which gives vendors stable revenue but also a responsibility not to exploit lock-in.
valueAndIncentives.example: A shop that adds a webshop and marketplace module roughly doubles its monthly fee.

valueAndIncentives.title: Ecosystem partners
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Payment, shipping, marketplace and accounting partners earn per transaction or subscription and depend on good connections with the till system.
valueAndIncentives.example: A marketplace connector charges per listing volume; a shipping platform per label.

challenges.title: Keeping stock true across channels
challenges.whyHard: Every channel changes stock at its own time, and some updates (deliveries, theft, damage) only happen when people record them.
challenges.tradeOff: Faster synchronisation costs more integration effort; slower sync risks overselling.
challenges.example: A marketplace sells the last tent before the shop sale reaches it, leading to a cancellation and a seller-rating penalty.
challenges.commonApproach: Real-time stock publication plus safety buffers on marketplaces; limited because buffers hide available stock.

challenges.title: Switching systems without disrupting the shop
challenges.whyHard: Years of articles, customers and history must move, and staff must relearn routines during trading hours.
challenges.tradeOff: A thorough migration takes time; a fast one risks dirty data.
challenges.example: Customer loyalty balances missing after go-live upset regulars.
challenges.commonApproach: Vendor-run migration and training before go-live; still dependent on the quality of the old data.

challenges.title: Branch-specific needs
challenges.whyHard: Bike shops need frame numbers and workshop planning, jewellers need gemstone specs and repairs, wholesalers need invoices.
challenges.tradeOff: Specialist features add complexity for shops that do not need them.
challenges.example: A general cloud POS cannot order from bike wholesalers inside the till.
challenges.commonApproach: Branch modules and supplier connections switched on per shop.

challenges.title: Growing out of the system
challenges.whyHard: A shop that becomes a chain with a large webshop needs warehouse and ERP features a POS-centred system may not have.
challenges.tradeOff: Changing to a heavier system adds cost and complexity; staying may limit growth.
challenges.example: A retailer with a large webshop considers a full commerce ERP.
challenges.commonApproach: Groups like Katapull offer an upgrade path to a sibling ERP; the boundaries between products must stay clear.

misconceptions.belief: A till system just takes payments.
misconceptions.reality: Payment is one step; most value is in stock, purchasing, customer and reporting data the till produces.

misconceptions.belief: Cloud means the shop cannot sell when the internet is down.
misconceptions.reality: It depends on the system; some keep local data so sales can continue and sync later. Shops should check this explicitly.

misconceptions.belief: Selling on marketplaces is just uploading products.
misconceptions.reality: Stock, prices and orders must stay synchronised continuously, or cancellations harm the shop's rating.

takeaways: Every sale is also a data event that updates stock, margin and customer history.
Stock accuracy connects the shop floor, the webshop and the marketplaces.
Supplier connections prevent errors at the source.
Specialty shops need branch-specific features such as repairs and serial numbers.
Choosing a system is a long-term decision because switching is costly.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why might a shop with an accurate till still oversell online?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Because online channels may receive stock changes with a delay.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Correct stock in the till is not enough if marketplaces or webshops are updated slowly; synchronisation speed matters.

knowledgeChecks.question: In the walkthrough, what prevented the margin loss after the supplier price change?
knowledgeChecks.answer: The supplier connection updated purchase prices and the system flagged low-margin items.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Margin depends on purchase price; automatic supplier data makes the change visible immediately.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a franchise head office need different tools than a single shop owner?
knowledgeChecks.answer: It must publish prices and campaigns to many independently owned shops and compare them.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Central control and consistent execution across shops is a different job from running one shop.
